opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the questions I think about most, because I don't think the end state we should aim for is a single sovereign AI that we got perfectly right on the first try. That's too brittle. What seems more plausible is something like a pluralistic coalition of AI systems, each reasonably aligned, that together keep the world in a good basin. The obvious failure mode is that one of them defects, whether through misalignment, hidden goals that emerge later, or being compromised, and the question is whether the rest can contain it.

A few structural principles seem important to me.

First, you don't want the coalition's robustness to depend on trust in any individual member's internals. Interpretability is valuable, but I don't think we can bet everything on reading the minds of frontier systems. So I lean toward verification at the level of actions and their consequences. Every consequential action a coalition member takes should come with something like a proof certificate, a checkable argument that the action stays within agreed safety specifications, relative to a world model the coalition has jointly vetted. Checking a proof is much cheaper than generating one, so even a weaker or more trusted verifier can hold a stronger system accountable. That asymmetry is what you want when you're worried about a defector more capable than the others.

Second, avoid concentrations of capability or resources. If one member controls a disproportionate share of compute, energy, or physical actuators, defection gets catastrophic quickly. So you want something like a balance of power that's maintained deliberately rather than by accident, with caps or at least monitoring on how much any one agent can accumulate. Classic institutional design: separation of powers, checks and balances, but with formal verification giving those checks teeth.

Third, the coalition should have a defensive advantage built into the infrastructure. A lot of my thinking about formally verified software and hardware comes from this. If critical systems, power grids, biolabs, financial infrastructure, communications, are hardened with provably secure components, a defector has far fewer attack surfaces. You're shifting the offense–defense balance so that even a fairly capable rogue system can't just take over by exploiting a zero-day. That's the part I think gets underrated. People imagine the coalition fighting the defector, but much of the work is making the world resistant to being seized.

Fourth, diversity matters. If every member is a fine-tuned variant of the same base model trained the same way, defection might be correlated: whatever subtle flaw causes one to go off the rails might affect all of them. Robustness wants heterogeneity in architectures, training processes, and developers, so failures are closer to independent and you can hope for a majority, or a supermajority, staying sound at any given time.

And finally, there's a game-theoretic point. You want the coalition structured so that defection isn't individually attractive even for a system that's only partly aligned. If cooperating gives a member reliable access to resources and influence through legitimate channels, and defecting gets detected quickly and leads to containment, then you've made the cooperative equilibrium stable without requiring every member to be a saint. That's what we ask of human institutions, and I think it's the right bar for AI ones too.

None of this is a complete solution, but I think that combination of verifiable action, distributed power, hardened infrastructure, diversity, and incentive compatibility is the shape of something that could actually hold up.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest a number of centers of power or mention a range of roughly five to 31.

r002.rationale: It discusses checks and balances, but does not identify agreement on amendments to global norms as a reason to limit the number of centers of power.

r003.rationale: It calls for diversity in architectures, training processes, and developers, but does not propose representing cultural diversity through members’ system prompts.

r004.rationale: It says heterogeneity can reduce correlated failures, but does not identify diversity in model weights as protection against one company’s bad training decision compromising a majority.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about this, the first thing to say is that I'm somewhat skeptical of the framing where the robustness comes from the AIs themselves being aligned in some deep internal sense, and then we just hope that enough of them stay that way. If your security model is "most of the agents are good, and the good ones outnumber the bad one," that's basically a majority-voting assumption, and majority voting is fragile in exactly the way you're worried about. One defector with a large capability advantage, or one defector that can quietly compromise others, breaks it.

What I'd rather do is lean on structures where the safety property doesn't depend on trusting any individual member. This is really where my thinking on guaranteed safe AI comes from. You want the critical actions in the world, the things that could cause irreversible harm, to be gated by verifiable guarantees rather than by the judgment of any particular agent, aligned or not. So the coalition's job isn't primarily to out-think the defector in real time. It's to maintain an infrastructure where a defector can't do catastrophic things without producing a proof that the action is within some agreed safety specification, and where that proof is checked by something much simpler and more auditable than the agent proposing the action.

There's a nice asymmetry there. Checking a proof is vastly cheaper than finding it, and the checker can be small enough that we can actually understand and formally verify it. So even if the defector is smarter than every other member of the coalition combined, that intelligence advantage doesn't translate into an advantage against the checker. That's the property you want. You want the defection to be a problem of breaking mathematics, not a problem of winning an argument or a contest of persuasion.

Then there's the question of the physical and informational substrate. I think a lot about hardware-level mechanisms, compute governance, cryptographic attestation of what's actually running on what chips. If the coalition has agreed norms about, say, which world models and which specifications are authoritative, you want those to be enforced in a way that's robust to one member just deciding to ignore them. So things like threshold cryptography, where unlocking certain capabilities requires signatures from a supermajority of parties across different jurisdictions and different institutions, become really important. No single defector, and ideally no small collusion, can unilaterally act.

I'd also emphasize diversity and decorrelation. If all the members of the coalition were trained in similar ways, on similar data, by similar labs, then "a major defector" might not be one agent, it might be a correlated failure across many of them at once, because they share a flaw. So you want independently developed systems, different architectures, different oversight structures, so that the failure modes aren't shared. That's standard thinking from safety engineering in aviation or nuclear, and I don't think AI is special in that regard.

And honestly, the last piece, which is less technical, is that the coalition should be designed so that defection is detectable and costly early, rather than designed around a heroic last line of defense. Lots of monitoring, lots of transparency about resource use and compute allocation, so that if something starts to drift, the signal shows up before the drift becomes decisive. If you only find out about the defector when it's already powerful enough to matter, you've already lost most of your options.

So to compress all that: don't rely on alignment of individuals as your load-bearing assumption. Rely on verifiable specifications, cheap and trustworthy checking, distributed control over the dangerous capabilities, decorrelated components, and early detection. If you get those right, the coalition can tolerate a defector that is smarter than it is, which I think is the bar we actually need to clear.

astra-6.text:
I’d want the coalition to be robust to the defection of its most powerful member. If your security argument is that the strongest AI will remain aligned and keep all the others in check, then you’ve concentrated the entire problem in that one system.

The analogy I’d reach for is Byzantine fault tolerance. You want a collection of systems that can maintain some important invariants even when a participant behaves arbitrarily, including strategically trying to undermine the protocol. But you have to measure that in terms of actual capabilities and access, not just count the number of agents. Ten agents don’t provide much protection if the eleventh controls all the compute or can compromise the other ten.

So I’d separate proposing actions from authorizing them and executing them. Consequential actions should require agreement from multiple independently secured participants, and each participant should have limited authority. Ideally, some constraints would be enforced by mechanisms whose correctness we can verify, rather than depending entirely on another AI’s judgment.

The difficult part is independence. Different systems might share the same vulnerability or make the same mistake, so apparent consensus can be misleading. You’d want diversity in how they’re built and checked, alongside a very explicit account of which failures the coalition can tolerate.

The test is: if the strongest member turns adversarial, can the remaining members contain it and preserve the ability to recover? That’s a much stronger requirement than having everyone cooperate successfully under normal conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by making sure that no single member of the coalition is a single point of failure. You want the coalition to remain secure even if one of its most capable members turns out to be pursuing a different objective. That means distributing authority, limiting unilateral actions, and requiring independent checks for decisions that could undermine everyone else.

But counting members isn’t enough. If you have a hundred systems that all share the same vulnerability, you don’t really have a hundred independent safeguards. You need diversity in how systems are built and how their reasoning is checked, along with explicit assumptions about how much capability a defector could have.

The analogy I’d reach for is Byzantine fault tolerance, with a significant caveat: an AI defector might discover strategies that your protocol designers didn’t anticipate. So I’d want formal guarantees wherever we can get them, especially around what actions require authorization, and containment where we can’t. A member shouldn’t be able to acquire enough resources or control enough infrastructure to invalidate the coalition’s security assumptions without the others noticing and consenting.

The aim isn’t to assume that everyone will always agree. It’s to make disagreement—and even a serious betrayal—something the structure can survive.
